perturbations.a: Atmospheric rivers (ARs) are international phenomena primarily occurring in the midlatitudes, distinguished by filamentary regions of robust horizontal water vapour transport in the atmosphere1,2,3,4,5,6,7. Firstly described by Newell et al.2, ARs are synoptic-scale filaments representing the 4 or 5 largest water vapour fluxes that occur between the midlatitudes and the tropics on any given day, and the length of an AR is typically five times its width. ARs frequently linked to extratropical cyclones and fronts4,5, the principal mechanisms of precipitation8,9, and play a critical role in extreme precipitation events10 in the midlatitudes. As part of extratropical cyclones and fronts, ARs have substantial hydrological impacts when making landfall for most mid-latitude regions globally, including extreme precipitation events11,12,13,14,15 and the frequency of the occurrence of droughts and floods16.

## Duke Mathematical Journal  

### The Sard hypothesis on Martinet surfaces  

#### Abstract  

Given a entirely nonholonomic distribution of rank $2$ on a $3$-dimensional manifold, we scrutinize the size of the set of points that can be attained by singular horizontal pathways starting from the same point. In this context, by the Sard hypothesis, that set should be a portion of the so-called Martinet surface of $2$-dimensional Hausdorff measure zero. We demonstrate that the hypothesis holds in the instance where the Martinet surface is smooth. Moreover, we tackle the instance of singular real-analytic Martinet surfaces, and we reveal that the result holds true under an assumption of nontransversality of the distribution on the singular set of the Martinet surface. Our techniques depend on the control of the divergence of vector fields generating the trace of the distribution on the Martinet surface and some methods of resolution of singularities.

# Is it feasible to connect leads to surface mount component?  

I requested an op amp to experiment with. I realized this was a surface mount component when I requested it. I presumed that I would be capable to somehow connect leads to it, so I could utilize it on my breadboard. Utilizing a simple soldering iron - is there a method I can connect leads to this component to utilize on my breadboard?  

I understand when these components are surface mounted they are only rated to come in contact with high temperatures for a moment or two. I was considering acquiring a small bead of solder on the end of a wire - getting the bead to liquify using the iron - then touching the wire and bead to one of the pins on the component (so the soldering iron doesn't touch the component directly).  

-  
Search on "dead bug protyping". It's most certainly achievable, and often a quick and simple solution to your problem. –  Scott Seidman Mar 23 '14 at 17:27  
A better image could have been achieved if you had positioned the thing on a white piece of paper and held the camera with both hands for steadiness and cleaner background. –  user1306322 Mar 23 '14 at 18:08  

@gerrishp2 25 pieces for less than $4 – alexan_e Mar 23 '14 at 17:22 You could connect leads but this isn't a particularly good idea, especially for use at moderate to high frequency. The last thing you want is wires dangling off it picking up noise or leading to oscillation. The same applies to breadboards, they are frequently not a good way to test high frequency, low noise opamps that are prone to go into oscillation without decent grounding. Some manufacturers sell evaluation boards designed to be used with surface mount opamps. For instance there are a range by TI stocked at a number of popular retailers. These boards are specifically designed for the surface mount opamps and have large ground planes that open up underneath the package body to minimize capacitance around the pins. Below is a picture of one I populated to test an opamp (before I cleaned it!). Alternatively, if you are using a general purpose opamp at low speed you could see if it is available in a DIP package. This would be a much better idea than tacking wires onto the easily damaged SMD legs, but still be cautious of using a breadboard for anything particularly sensitive. - +1 Nice, thanks for that. At$5 each, worth having a few around, even with lots of the other kinds of adapters. –  Spehro Pefhany Mar 22 '14 at 17:50

# Structural evidence theory

In mathematical reasoning, structural evidence theory is the subdiscipline of evidence theory that examines evidence calculi that support a concept of analytic evidence.

## Analytic evidence

Main article: analytic evidence

The concept of analytic evidence was introduced into evidence theory by Gerhard Gentzen for the sequent calculus; the analytic evidence are those that are cut-free. His natural deduction calculus also supports a concept of analytic evidence, as was shown by Dag Prawitz; the definition is slightly more intricate we say the analytic evidence are the normal forms, which are related to the concept of normal form in term rewriting.

## Structures and connectives

The term structure in structural evidence theory comes from a technical concept introduced in the sequent calculus: the sequent calculus represents the judgement made at any stage of an inference using special, extra-logical operators which we call structural operators: in , the commas to the left of the turnstile are operators normally interpreted as conjunctions, those to the right as disjunctions, whilst the turnstile symbol itself is interpreted as an implication. However, it is important to note that there is a fundamental difference in behaviour between these operators and the logical connectives they are interpreted by in the sequent calculus: the structural operators are used in every rule of the calculus, and are not considered when asking whether the subformula property applies. Furthermore, the logical rules go one way only: logical structure is introduced by logical rules, and cannot be eliminated once created, while structural operators can be introduced and eliminated in the course of a derivation.

The idea of looking at the syntactic features of sequents as special, non-logical operators is not old, and was forced by innovations in evidence theory: when the structural operators are as simple as in Getzen's original sequent calculus there is little need to analyse them, but evidence calculi of deep inference such as display logic support structural operators as complex as the logical connectives, and demand sophisticated treatment.

## Cut-elimination in the sequent calculus

Main article: Cut-elimination

## Natural deduction and the formulae-as-types correspondence

Main article: Natural deduction

## Logical duality and harmony

Main article: Logical harmony

## References

• Sara Negri; Jan Von Plato (2001). Structural evidence theory. Cambridge University Press. ISBN 978-0-521-79307-0.
• Anne Sjerp Troelstra; Helmut Schwichtenberg (2000). Basic evidence theory (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. ISBN 978-0-521-77911-1.

## Topological algebras. Chosen topics.(English)Zbl 0597.46046

North-Holland Mathematics Studies, 124. Notas de Matemática, 109. Amsterdam etc.: North-Holland. XVII, 535 p. \$ 64.75; Dfl. 175.00 (1986).  
The general notion of a normed algebra was introduced in 1936 by M. Nagumo. The examination of ideals in normed algebras was accomplished by I. Gel’fand in a series of papers published in 1941. The topological embedding of what we call today a $$C^*$$-algebra into the algebra of linear bounded operators on a Hilbert space was demonstrated in 1943 by I. Gel’fand and M. A. Naĭmark. These are some of the primary stages which led to the advancement of the contemporary Banach algebra theory.  
Nevertheless, the presence of topological algebras that are not normed, which are of interest for both the theory and applications, has compelled the mathematicians to explore the possibility of adjustment of the framework of Banach algebra theory to more general situations. The present book is devoted to such explorations. The first part of the book addresses the general theory of topological algebras, in particular of locally convex ones. Topological tensor products of topological algebras are introduced in the second part of the book. The author attempted, and we think that he succeeded, to state the theorems in their ”most useful generality”. The book also includes a large variety of examples. The occurrence of monographs dedicated to this subject is a necessity and many specialists in functional analysis will appreciate the present work.  
Reviewer: F.-H.Vasilescu

### MSC:

 46H05 General theory of topological algebras 46M05 Tensor products in functional analysis 46-02 Research exposition (monographs, survey articles) pertaining to functional analysis

# Is moment a Scalar or a Vector?

In Wikipedia it's said that moment is a scalar quantity. But its hard to comprehend that how? As stated that we consider only the magnitude of moment then its a scalar. But on basis of moment we define yesterday, today and tomorrow then what it will be?

-  
If it was a vector, what would its direction be? – Martin Büttner Apr 2 '13 at 10:54  
@Martin forward, obviously! – rubenvb Jun 18 '15 at 12:22  

To pick up on twistor59's point, moment is not a vector but a time interval is.

The confusion arises because you have to define carefully what you mean by the word moment. In special relativity we label spacetime points by their co-ordinates $(t, x, y, z)$, where $t$ is the moment co-ordinate. The numbers $t$, $x$, etc are not themselves vectors because they just label positions in spacetime. So in this sense the moment co-ordinate, $t$, is not a vector any more than the spatial co-ordinates are.

But we often use the word moment to mean a time interval, and in this sense the moment is the vector joining the spacetime points $(t, x, y, z)$ and $(t + t', x, y, z)$, where $t'$ is the time interval you measure with your stopwatch between the two points. The interval between the two points is $(t', 0, 0, 0)$ and this is a vector.

-  
Yep good point. Wiki could do with a little bit of caveating of their phrase in order to avoid these confusions. – twistor59 Apr 2 '13 at 13:30  

In physics101, scalar quantities are defined to be ones which have magnitude only, and no direction, where "direction" in this context means a direction in three dimensional space. Moment clearly has no such direction.

However, in slightly more advanced physics, where special relativity is applied "scalar" is used as a shorthand for "Lorentz scalar" - a quantity which does not change under Lorentz transformations. Moment most certainly does change under Lorentz transformations, so is not a scalar in this context.

-  
twistor59, If you imagine moment to be one dimensional and therefore linear, then moment can be a vector quantity. Even if it only has two possible directions that it can go. However, I think personally that moment should be classified as a pseudo-vector, as it can be measured both as a scalar and as a vector. – user42646 Mar 16 '14 at 10:19  
Well, numbers are vectors too.Since they belong to the vector space $\mathbb{R}^1$. Pseudo-vector is a misleading term, because it has a specific meaning (axial vector). – jinawee Mar 16 '14 at 12:04  

A vector is a scalar with direction. So moment can be a vector, but what it means depends on the context. In 1D it has only 2 directions, positive and negative with zero being positive. In 2D it can be an angle between ÷/-Pi radians. And so on.

Moment can be a single dimension attached to the familiar 3 Euclidean spatial dimensions and in this case it is arbitrarily deemed to be a scalar until people wonder why moment doesn't go backwards. The answer to that annoying inane question is that relativistic moment is a 3D vector property of 3D space, not a scalar attached to it. And vectors do not sensibly take on negative values. For example look outside at a flag pole and tell me if the flag is blowing backward or forward or not at all? It's a nonsense question right? Because the wind blows or it doesn't, and it blows in a direction with a positive value.

The terms backwards and forwards cannot be used to describe the wind. Neither does real moment go backward or forward, but merely faster or slower.

And so when you move in space relativistically, the passage of moment in each frame of reference of nearby objects will vary according to the various directions of motion (moment vectors) and their various instantaneous locations in relation to each other.

-

# Total of random variables - Verify your derived distribution against a numerical computation/histogram

Consider separate random variates $$X_0, X_1, . . .$$ each uniformly distributed on the support $$[0, 1)$$

Let's say $$Y = X_0 + X_1$$, where $$X_0$$ and $$X_1$$ are separate uniform random variables with range $$[0,1)$$

I then deduced the following PDF to depict the distribution of the total $$Y = X_0 + X_1$$ using a convolution.

$$f(y) = \begin{cases} y & \text{for 0 < y < 1} \\ 2-y & \text{for 1 \le y < 2} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$

I want to verify the derived distribution against a numerical computation/histogram (in python)

Any assistance is appreciated

import numpy as np  
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  
  
X_0 = np.random.uniform(0.0,1.0,1000)  
X_1 = np.random.uniform(0.0,1.0,1000)  
  
Y = X_0 + X_1  
  
#Plot 3 normalized histograms  
plt.hist(X_0,bins=100,density=True)  
plt.hist(X_1,bins=100,density=True)  
plt.hist(Y,bins=100,density=True)  
  
#desired distribution  
if 0<Y<1:  
F_Y = Y  
if 1<=Y<2:  
F_Y = 2 - Y  
if Y < 0:  
F_Y = 0  
  
plt.plot(Y,F_Y)  
plt.title('desired distribution')  
plt.show()

import numpy as np

def show_histogram(vals):  
n, bins, patches = plt.hist(x=vals, bins='auto', density=True, color='#0504aa', alpha=0.7, rwidth=0.85)  
plt.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.75)  
plt.xlabel('Value')  
plt.ylabel('Frequency')  
plt.title('Distribution of computed values')  
  
X_0 = np.random.uniform(0.0,1.0,10000)  
X_1 = np.random.uniform(0.0,1.0,10000)  
  
Y = X_0 + X_1

show_histogram(X_0+X_1)  
  
#desired distribution  
n=100  
Y = 2*np.arange(n)/(n-1)  
F_Y=1.0 - np.abs(Y-1)  
  
plt.plot(Y,F_Y)  
plt.title('desired distribution')  
plt.show()

# StackFck2d  
  
95 views  
  
As you may or may not be aware, I've always been fascinated by languages/compilers/interpreters so I did my weekly x hour codeathon (this weekend it was 2 hours)...and StackFck2d was created!  
  
Its just like Brainfck but with 6 new commands...here is the full listing of commands:  
>	moves the pointer east.<	moves the pointer west.^	moves the pointer north.v	moves the pointer south.+	increment (increase by one) the value(top of the stack) at the pointer.-	decrement (decrease by one) the value(top of the stack) at the pointer..	output the value of the byte(top of the stack) at the pointer.,	accept one byte of input, storing its value in the top of the stack at the pointer.[	jump forward to the command after the corresponding ] if the byte at the pointer is zero.]	jump back to the command after the corresponding [ if the byte at the pointer is nonzero.@	pushes an empty cell onto the top of the location's stack#	pops the topmost cell off of the location's stack%	copies the current location's value and places it into the global variable&	pastes the global variable's value into the current location's value  
  
Now, let me clarify the new aspects. Its not 1d like BF, this is 2d. You can move in 4 directions instead of 2. Also, each "cell" is now a stack. When you use + and -, you influence the top of the stack. There are also 2 commands for copying and pasting cells.  
  
I did this in 2 hours so the code is unattractive, crammed into 2 functions, and may not function 100%! The loops are the only aspect that may not operate perfectly, but from my few tests, they worked. Here is the compiler with source:  
StackFuck2d.zip  
  
I know its not a lot and doesn't add much magnificence to BF, but I wanted a project to experiment with in a brief amount of time and learn some things about the STL. Have fun  
  
;)  
  
There are no comments to show.

Maybe you mean a complex manifold $M$ of dimension $n$ is balanced iff it admits a hermitian metric $\omega$ satisfying $d\omega^{n-1}=0$.

In the paper:Metric properties of manifolds bimeromorphic to compact Kahler spaces. (JDG.v37.1993.95-121), L. Alessandrini and G. Bassanelli had demonstrated the following result:

Let $M$ and $N$ be compact complex manifolds and $f:N\longrightarrow M$ be a modification, then 1) $M$ is balanced $\Longrightarrow N$ is balanced. 2) $N$ is balanced and satisfies a cohomological condition (it 's called B in the above paper)$\Longrightarrow M$ is balanced.

For the details, you should read their paper.

In addition, if you mean "balance" in the Kahler-Einstein problem, the following two papers maybe beneficial.

a) S.K. DONALDSON: SCALAR CURVATURE AND PROJECTIVE EMBEDDINGS I

b）CLAUDIO AREZZO AND FRANK PACARD: BLOWING UP AND DESINGULARIZING CONSTANT SCALAR CURVATURE KAHLER MANIFOLDS

# Refactoring durability  

305 glimpses  

I had a touch of pressure at my dayjob this spring with a lot of extra hours, so I kinda lost the enthusiasm for working on my game. This last week I've been getting back into the game again. Since I've kinda forgotten a lot about working in Unity I wanted to begin on something that I could do purely serverside (C#) - refactoring how storage is being managed. I was already executing database operations asynchronously, but it was a bit awkward and not even implemented securely. DB tasks were (sometimes) being enqueued in a thread-safe manner, but they were referencing live game entities themselves, thereby sharing them between the game logic and database layer, without any locks, mutexes or other synchronization constructs - OUCH!  
Other times blocking DB queries were being issued directly by the code that managed network messages from the client (login, create player etc.). Obviously this would starve the networking thread pool for no reason, and also result in DB queries waiting on locks - also ouch...  

Basically it was all a bit of a jumble. I wanted to shift more towards a share-nothing framework, and a single writing DB thread. I have to give credits to It-Hare (Sergey Ignatchenko) for his motivational articles. He's penning a multi-volume book on MMO development and has a lot of early versions of the articles for his book freely accessible on his website.  
A couple of articles with significance to what I'm doing atm:  
http://ithare.com/eight-ways-to-handle-non-blocking-returns-in-message-passing-programs-with-script/  

I also wanted to be capable of batching logical transactions in a single database transaction, allowing me to:  

1. Issue batch updates and inserts  

2. Reduce the amount of transaction logfile thrashing  

This would afford me a higher potential throughput at the cost of some latency which doesn't trouble me as long as the player is able to log in within a few seconds. The game itself never waits for database transactions anyway, so these "few seconds" are an acceptable upper limit for latency of DB transactions.  

In addition to that I wanted an architecture that could accommodate moving the DB server to another computer.  

This increased latency would of course make any blocking calls to the DB an even bigger No-No than it already was, so reading the articles (among others) mentioned before motivated me to have a single thread for durability, with logical database transactions being placed into a queue (coupled with continuation lambdas) to be batched up and executed.  

So I made a durability server with an app-level cache where transactions can be queued and a single DB update thread that just pulls transactions from the queue, executes them, commits the batch and returns the outcomes of the transactions to the caller.  
To be honest this has not (yet) been implemented as a server but just as an in-process object with an Enqueue() method and an OnResult() event. I don't know which communication protocol I would utilize - Rest, homebrew TCP, something entirely different? But I don't want to bother with it now anyway since it is not important at this stage and whatever I choose would probably be altered anyway. I also decided not to decide on a storage technology. My old DAL layer used SQLite but I want to get rid of that third part dependency for now so I'll just be saving JSON files to avoid having to update schemas with frequent data changes. I'm actually not even doing that yet - I'm just using the app-level cache itself which means nothing is preserved on program exit.  
I then made a PersistenceController that will execute on the gameserver.  
It has methods like LoginAccount, UpdatePlayerCharacter etc. In addition to the normal parameters they also take Action/ Action<T> parameters so you can provide a lambda expression to act as a continuation on completion of a transaction.  
These methods just enqueue the transactions, letting another thread handle the transmitting of the transactions to the durability server. This transaction transmitting is also being done in batches from the controller to cut down on ping-pong - these batches do not nece  
Mutable reference-type parameters (basically anything heavier than a String or an int) are mapped to DTOs before being enqueued, so that no live game data is shared between threads.  

Time for a little code, showing how the handling of a request for availability of an account name resulted in a blocking call to the database. Fine for serving an individual client with low latency but blocking a thread on the iocp pool for several milliseconds? A dreadful idea in a multi-player game.  

Notice SendMessage doesn't in fact send anything - it just queues the message for sending.  

public override void Execute(NetworkMessage message, ServerConnection con)  
{  
bool accountNameAvailable = !PlayerDataMapper.AccountExists(name);  
con.SendMessage(ServerMessageFactory.CreateAccountNameAvailableResponse(name, accountNameAvailable));  
}  

Here is the same code using the durability controller, with the continuation as a lambda expression.  

public override void Execute(NetworkMessage message, ServerConnection con)  
{  
PersistenceController.AccountExists(name, exists =>  
{  
bool accountNameAvailable = !exists;  
con.SendMessage(ServerMessageFactory.CreateAccountNameAvailableResponse(name, accountNameAvailable));  
});  
}

## Sunday, March 19, 2006

### To Infinity... And Beyond! Topic: Algebra/Inequalities. Level: Olympiad.

Problem: (1996 Ireland - #7) Prove that for all positive whole numbers $n$,

$2^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot 4^{\frac{1}{4}} \cdots (2^n)^{\frac{1}{2^n}} < 4$.

Solution: Clearly, the product grows, so if we demonstrate that the infinite product is equal to $4$, we know that the partial products must always be lower than $4$. Rewrite the infinite product as

$2^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot 2^{\frac{2}{4}} \cdot 2^{\frac{3}{8}} \cdots$.

We wish to demonstrate that

$\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{4}+\frac{3}{8} \cdots = 2$.

We can rewrite it as the addition of an infinite number of infinite geometric series, or

$\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\cdots\right)+\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\cdots\right)+\cdots$,

which becomes

$1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\cdots = 2$.

Hence the infinite product is equal to $2^2 = 4$ and the partial products are $< 4$ as desired. QED.

--------------------

Comment: With powers, a lot of the time it's a good idea to look at the powers themselves because it usually reduces the problem to a sum instead of a product, which is simpler to work with.

--------------------

Practice Problem: Assess $n^{\frac{1}{n}} \cdot (n^2)^{\frac{1}{n^2}} \cdot (n^3)^{\frac{1}{n^3}} \cdots$.

which becomes

$1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\cdots = 2$.

Hence the infinite product is the same as $2^2 = 4$ and the partial products are $< 4$ as desired. QED.

--------------------

Comment: With exponents, frequently it's a good idea to check the exponents themselves because it generally reduces the issue to a sum instead of a product, which is simpler to manage.

The dilemma statement, all variables and provided/recognized data Two non-conductive spheres have radii r1 and r2, weights m1 and m2, and uniformly distributed charges -q1 and q2. They are released from rest when their centers are distanced by a gap d. How swift is each moving when they collide? Suggestion: Consider conservation of energy and of linear momentum. 2. Relevant formulas I thought these were relevant: Momentum=mv Kinetic energy = 1/2(mv^2) $$\Delta$$U = -q$$\int$$E dr 3. The attempt at a resolution First I solved for the potential energy that this system gains when the two spheres are moved apart: $$\Delta$$U = q1$$\int^{d}_{d-r1-r2}$$E dr = k(q1)(q2)($$\frac{1}{d-r1-r2}$$ - 1/d) I figured this is the amount of energy the spheres would possess when they collide, so... $$\Delta$$U = $$\frac{1}{2}$$(m1)v$$^{2}_{1}$$ + $$\frac{1}{2}$$(m2)v$$^{2}_{2}$$ From conservation of momentum, v2 = (m1/m2)v1 so substituting that into the above equation I got: $$\Delta$$U = $$\frac{1}{2}$$m1v$$^{2}_{1}$$ + $$\frac{1}{2}$$$$\frac{m^{2}_{1}}{m_{2}}$$v$$^{2}_{1}$$ So then I solved for v1 to obtain: v1 = $$\sqrt{\frac{2kq_{1}q_{2}((1/(d-r1-r2)-(1/d))}{m_{1}+\frac{m^{2}_{1}}{m_{2}}}}$$ And v2 can be determined the same way. However, I know for a certainty this isn't the correct answer. In closing, I don't really know what I did incorrect, but I suspect it's because I treated the two spheres as point charges, and I'm not certain if I'm justified in doing that.

## Summary  

This document proposes a new algorithm which enables us to train a deep neural network under a modest privacy budget. It provides protection against a strong adversary with full knowledge of the training mechanism and access to the model's parameters.

## The Algorithm  

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1607.00133.pdf  
The algorithm is very comparable to the traditional SGD algorithm with few exceptions:  
1. 1.  
To assure our model is differentially private, we need to limit the influence of each individual example on our model. Thus, we clip each gradient in l2 norm.  
2. 2.  
The algorithm adds noise at lot-level. Lots are analogous to batches, but, to restrict the memory consumption, we may set the batch size much smaller than the lot size. We perform the computation in batches, then group several batches into a lot for adding noise.  
3. 3.  
The algorithm computes the overall privacy cost of the training.

Two procedures to calculate the maximal quantity of leaves in induced subtrees  
Élise Vandomme  

Subtrees of graphs, as well as their quantity of leaves, have been explored by various communities: from discrete mathematics to data mining and information retrieval. We consider a variant where we require the subtrees to be induced and calculate their maximal quantity of leaves. The issue, which is NP-complete in general, becomes polynomial in the case of trees. The leaf function associates to a quantity $n$ the maximal quantity of leaves an induced subtree of size $n$ can have. To calculate the leaf function, we provide an efficient branch and bound procedure. In the particular case of trees, we describe a polynomial procedure using the dynamic programming paradigm. We conclude by exhibiting a link between the leaf functions of caterpillar graphs and a particular class of words called prefix normal.

# Convergence of $\sqrt[n]{s_n}$ given $s_ns_m \leq s_{n+m}$

Given $(s_n)_{n \geq 1}$, a series of positive integers and the inequality $s_ns_m \leq s_{n+m}$ for all integers $n, m$, how does one proceed to proving that the series $(\sqrt[n]{s_n})_{n \geq 1}$ converges?

It is quite straightforward to see that the series is monotone increasing, so all we need is an upper bound for all of its terms. I don't quite understand how to do this, since the inequality only seems to provide a lower bound..

Consider the series $s_n = 2^{n^2}$ and observe that \begin{align} s_ns_m = 2^{n^2+m^2} \leq 2^{(m+n)^2}= s_{n+m} \end{align} but we see that \begin{align} \sqrt[n]{s_n} = 2^n\rightarrow \infty. \end{align}

# 1979 BootstrapTechniques

Subject Headings: Bootstrapped Resampling, Quenouille — Tukey jackknife; Jackknifing.

## Quotes

### Abstract

We explore the following issue: given a random sample $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, X_2, ..., X_n)$ from an unknown probability distribution $F$, estimate the sampling distribution of some predetermined random variable $R(\mathbf{X}, F)$, on the basis of the observed data $\mathbf{x}$. (Standard jackknife theory provides an approximate mean and variance in the instance $R(\mathbf{X},F)=\theta(\hat{F})-\theta(F), \theta$ some parameter of interest.) A general approach, termed the “bootstrap," is presented, and shown to function satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is indicated to be a linear approximation approach for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds through a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

### 1. Introduction

The Quenouille — Tukey jackknife is an interesting non-parametric approach for estimating the bias and variance of a statistic of interest, and also for testing the null hypothesis that the distribution of a statistic is centered at some predetermined point. ...

perturbations.c: # Some flat isospectral regions
perturbations.d: The creators give a number of instances of two noncongruent isospectral areas in the plane and a particularly straightforward method of demonstration. One of their instances is a pair of areas that are not only isospectral but homophonic, i.e. each area has a distinguished point such that the corresponding normalized Dirichlet eigenfunctions take equal values at the distinguished points. They interpret this to mean that if the corresponding drums'' are struck at these special points, then they sound the same'' in the very strong sense that every frequency will be excited to the same intensity for each. This illustrates that one really cannot perceive the shape of a drum.

perturbations.a: If two shapes have all three pairs of corresponding angles identical, then the shapes are identical.
perturbations.b: If two figures have all three pairs of corresponding angles equal, then the figures are equal.

### Comparison of Diverse AUSM Type Schemes for the Two-Fluid Model  
  
Steinar Evje and Tore Flåtten  
  
Abstract: In this article we make additional examinations of the {\em Mixture Flux} (MF) method for two-phase flows originally established in the framework of the AUSMD scheme \cite{evj03}. Here we utilize the method in conjunction with nonlinear state relations. We tackle stability and precision issues related to the discretization of the pressure terms, and propose a modification that permits a less strict stability criterion on the timestep. We further employ the framework to the two-phase AUSM$^+$ scheme of Paill\`{e}re et al (2003, Comput. Fluids~{\bf 32}, 891--916), denoting the resulting scheme as MF-AUSM$^+$. Comparisons between the previously constructed MF-AUSMD \cite{evj03} as well as the original AUSM$^+$ are made through numerical trials. In particular, we notice that the MF-AUSM$^+$ offers substantial enhancements in robustness over the original AUSM$^+$.

## Cryptology ePrint Archive: Report 2017/907

On differential correspondence of APN functions

Anastasiya Gorodilova

Abstract: For a specified vectorial Boolean function $F$ from $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ to itself it was defined an related Boolean function $\gamma_F(a,b)$ in $2n$ variables by C. Carlet, P. Charpin, V. Zinoviev in 1998 that takes value $1$ iff $a\neq{\bf 0}$ and equation $F(x)+F(x+a)=b$ has solutions. In this paper we introduce the concept of differentially corresponding functions as vectorial functions that have identical associated Boolean functions. To describe differential correspondence class of a specified APN function is an open problem of significant interest. We obtained that each quadratic APN function $G$ in $n$ variables, $n\leq 6$, that is differentially corresponding to a specified quadratic APN function $F$, is represented as $G = F + A$, where $A$ is an affine function. For the APN Gold function $F(x)=x^{2^k+1}$, where gcd$(k,n)=1$, we fully described all affine functions $A$ such that $F$ and $F+A$ are differentially corresponding. This result implies that APN Gold functions $F$ with $k=n/2 - 1$ for $n=4t$ form the initial infinitive family of functions up to EA-equivalence having non-trivial differential correspondence class consisting of more than $2^{2n}$ trivial functions $F_{c,d}(x) = F(x+c)+d$, $c,d\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

Category / Keywords: foundations / Boolean function, Almost perfect nonlinear function, Almost bent function, Crooked function, Differential correspondence, Linear spectrum

# Influence of coagulation of vertices in an advancing intricate network  

#### The authors emphasize on scale-free networks,  

with reference to Moore et al’s model which comprises obliteration of nodes. They examine a Japanese business association network. Companies are established, develop, cease, and merge. Firms have (observed and quantifiable) preferential attachment to firms with higher degree.  

(a) The three fundamental processes. (b) Time progression of the number of connections. (c) Lifetime and average degree. (d) Cumulative distribution of the number of connections, with c=0 (orange) to c=0.5 (blue).  

The cumulative distribution of company lifetimes is exponential $P(\geq t) \propto \exp(-t/\tau),$ where $\tau=18.8$ years. (we see similar trends in speciation). A semi-log plot demonstrates degree grows exponentially with lifetime, where expected degree is $\exp(At)$ and $A=0.017$.  

This indicates the degree distribution should be power-law with exponent $1/A\tau$, or 3.1. The observed degree distribution has exponent 1.3. Conclusion: random obliteration and growth by preferential attachment do not clarify the real world.  

To clarify this, the authors shift to coagulation models of aerosols and colloids; the mass of these clouds follows a power law. They propose a model where network vertices can merge. More specifically, starting with N vertices, evolve the network by stochastically selecting obliteration, creation, or coagulation at each time step, with probabilities a, b, c ($b=a+c=0.5$). With 10^5 vertices, the model stabilizes after 10^7 iterations, suggesting one year in the real world == 10600 iterations.  

They illustrate, both analytically and by simulation that the coagulation likelihood governs the final configuration of the degree distribution. Small $c$ yields an exponential distribution, large $c$ yields power law.  

Phys. Rev. Lett. 108, 168701 (2012) Influence of Coagulation of Vertices in an Advancing Intricate Network. Wataru Miura, Hideki Takayasu, and Misako Takayasu

# Disparity of confined linear operators on Hilbert space  

Let $T$ and $S$ be confined linear operators on a Hilbert space $H$. Verify that: $||TS||\leq ||T||\cdot ||S||$.  

The definition of the operator's norm is $||T||=\sup\{||Tv||_H: ||v||_H=1\}$.  

Thanks for your assistance.  

-  
This is one of the most elementary properties of confined linear operators in a normed space - in fact, it's true in numerous other norms than the one you presented. You should just consider it for a minute; the proof is a one-liner (often the awareness that the proof is elementary is sufficient to help spur you along to the answer). – Sargera Dec 2 '12 at 3:26  
You are correct. Thanks. – Hiperion Dec 2 '12 at 3:32  
add comment  

## 1 Response  

Note that for any $x\in H$, $\|Sx\|\leq\|S\|\|x\|$ and similarly $\|Ty\|\leq\|T\|\|y\|$ for any $y\in H$. Thus we have, for any $v$ with $\|v\|=1$, $$\|TSv\|\leq\|T\|\|Sv\|\leq\|T\|\|S\|\|v\|=\|T\|\|S\|$$

Would a Rubik's cube be a trapdoor function?

It's simple to scramble a Rubik's cube but it is challenging to solve, unless you know the algorithms for resolving it. This makes it a trapdoor function, correct?

• No, it does not. Scrambling a Rubik is the same as symmetric encryption. – ThoriumBR Feb 1 '16 at 14:02
• But I know an algorithm to resolve it without knowing the "encryption key" of the scramble. – Hurricane996 Feb 1 '16 at 14:06
• The algorithm to resolve the Rubik can be considered bruteforcing it, while doing the shuffle backwards would be the proper decryption. – ThoriumBR Feb 1 '16 at 14:22
• Really? I thought you would do – Hurricane996 Feb 1 '16 at 15:16
• The algorithm to resolve a cube is not brute forcing it — trying every possible permutation is. The algorithm to resolve a cube is equivalent to a catastrophic known-plaintext cryptanalytic attack against the "Rubiks cipher". – Stephen Touset Feb 1 '16 at 22:54

For a low number of n where n is the number of rotate-operations executed on the cube, it is true that finding a solution for the cube is more computationally expensive than applying the rotations. But with very high values of n this may change. It was proven that any rubic's cube configuration can be resolved with 20 moves or less, and finding that 20 move sequence might in fact be quicker than applying the "correct" sequence.

Let $u_0 \in L^\infty(\Omega)$ and $f \in L^\infty((0,T)\times\Omega)$ and consider $$u_t - \Delta u = f$$ $$u(0) = u_0$$ with some boundary constraints. Consider the weak form

$$\int_{\Omega}u_t\varphi + \int_{\Omega}\nabla u \nabla \varphi = \int_{\Omega}f\varphi$$

How can I demonstrate that $u \in {L^\infty((0,T)\times \Omega)}$ or $u \in {L^\infty(0,T;L^\infty(\Omega))}$, without utilizing classical method (just a weak method)?

If the classical theory cannot be circumvented then I don’t mind employing it. I would have thought we should evaluate with $(u(t) - \Vert u_0 \Vert_{L^\infty})^+$ but don’t know what to do with the term involving $f$.

Consider some $v(t) = \alpha t + \beta$. Then $v(t)$ will fulfill $$v_t - \Delta v = \alpha,\\ v(0) = \beta.$$ Take now $\alpha$ such that $\alpha \geq f$ in $(0, T)\times \Omega$ and $\beta$ such that $\beta \geq u(0)$. (it is feasible due to the boundedness of $f$ and $u_0$).
Therefore, the Weak maximum principle for $w = v - u$ will give you that $w \geq 0$. Hence, $u \leq v$, but $v$ is confined (for $T < +\infty$). Thus, $u$ is also confined.

# Symposium at SMU Delhi

June 28, 2011 (Tuesday), 3:30 PM at Webinar  
Speaker: Apoorva Khare, Stanford University, USA  
Title: Generalizing the concept of convexity: weak facets of weight polytopes  
Abstract of Talk  
The concept of convexity and facets of polytopes is well recognized: a subset is a facet if it maximizes a linear functional, and also if and only if it complies with a condition involving convex linear combinations. In joint work with Chari and Ridenour, we broaden this concept to arbitrary subsets of Euclidean space and arbitrary subfields of coefficients (in the convex combinations). We then utilize this to identify and classify facets'' of the set of lattice points within weight polytopes connected to finite-dimensional modules over complex semisimple Lie algebras.

# pull boundary conditions in elasticity  

I possess a question concerning executing pull boundary conditions in 2D and 3D linear elasticity. Contemplate the image above. I desire to impose pull boundary conditions on the boundary in crimson. My query is: How is the node sequence/connectivity for the pull elements characterized? In 2D the boundary term $$({\bf{w}},{\bf{h}})_{\Gamma_h}$$ is a line integral. Since the connectivity for elements 3 and 4 is (5,6,9,8) and (4,5,8,7) should the nodes for the pull elements be selected in the same sequence? That is, should the four pull elements possess the connectivity (6,9), (9,8), (8,7) and (7,4)? That indicates the boundary integral should be $$\int_{node 6}^{node 9} {\bf{w}}\cdot{\bf{h}} \,d\Gamma$$ and correspondingly for the others?  

What is the circumstance in 3D? In 3D the pull elements are bilinear quads (for trilinear hex elements). Is the connectivity of pull elements in 3D specified so that the normal points outward according to the right hand principle? So for the right most face element in the above image, should the connectivity be (3,7,6,2) and for the uppermost face element the connectivity should be (7,8,5,6)?  

• I'm quite confident that the orientation of integration is inconsequential. For 2D elasticity, I believe that the boundary term $(w,h)_\Gamma_h$ is a line integral. The definition of a line integral renders the orientation of integration inconsequential. In 3D, the boundary term is a surface integral and I think it must be specified in a manner analogous to the line integral. – Nachiket Sep 8 at 5:57  

## 1 Answer  

It relies on the execution. More than the connectivity, you need to center on the orientation of the normals.  

The common standard is to characterize the connectivity such that the normals on the boundary elements face away from the solid. This is comparatively simple in 2D since there are only two nodes for one (linear) element.  

For 3D, select the connectivity for the face element based on the node numbering for the quad element in 2D. Note that the boundary integral on a 2D face in 3D is nothing but the area integral for the quad element in 2D. Once you select the sequencing standard for the nodes, then you need to verify the orientation of the normals. If you reverse the arrangement of the nodes, then the direction of the normal will be in contrary direction. For instance, the normal on the face with node arrangement 1-2-3-4 is in contrary direction to that of the face with node arrangement 4-3-2-1. This can get intricate if you produce meshes independently.  

For producing meshes, I recommend utilizing some established mesh generators, for example, GMSH, TetGen or Hypermesh, since they supply boundary elements with consistent node arrangement.

perturbations.a:
# How do you obtain the likelihood distribution for $I$?

I'm perusing a book. On pages 105 and 106 it is mentioned that:

For N-look intensity SAR images,  
$$I_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N I_1(i)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x(i)^2+y(i)^2)$$  

Where $x(i)$ and $y(i)$ are the real of the $i$th look (or sample). Since $x(i)$ and $y(i)$ are independently Gaussian distributed, it is well known that $NI_N$ has a Chi-square distribution with $2N$ degrees of liberty. Therefore, the PDF of the N-look intensity is characterized by $$p_N(I)=\frac{N^N I^{N-1}}{(N-1)!\sigma^{2N}}\exp(-\frac{NI}{\sigma^2}),\quad I\ge 0$$  
The mean and the variance are $M_N(I)=\sigma^2$ and $\text{Var}_N(I)=\frac{\sigma^4}{N}$, respectively.

I don't have any issue with $NI_N$ possessing a chi-square distribution with $2N$ degrees of liberty but as we know the PDF for a chi-square distribution with $f$ degrees of liberty is:  
$$h(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2^{\frac{f}{2}}\Gamma(\frac{f}{2})}x^{\frac{(f-2)}{2}}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\quad &, x\ge 0\\[2ex] 0\quad &, x\lt 0 \end{cases}$$  
so for the distribution of $NI$ we should have:  
$$p(NI)=\frac{1}{2^N\Gamma(N)}(NI)^{N-1}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})=\frac{N^{N-1}I^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})$$  
Then if we regard $Y=NI$ as a function of $I$, we have:  
$$p(Y)\,dY=p(I)\,dI\;,\;dY=N\,dI\\\frac{N^{N-1}I^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})NdI=p(I)dI\\p(I)=\frac{N^NI^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})$$  
Then where does that $\sigma^2$ arise from instead of $2$?  
As far as I am aware degree of liberty ($f$) is the only parameter of chi-square distribution. and the mean and the variance of this distribution are $f$ and $2f$ respectively as wiki page states.

I do not know the context, but I would presume that gaussian distribution in the book are not scaled, so their variance is not equal to $1$. Therefore you have another parameter $\sigma^2$.  
So what you obtain is not exactly chi-squared distribution, but chi-squared scaled by a constant. Think of it as Gamma distribution with shape parameter $N$ and scale parameter $\sigma^2/N$.

# How do you create the probability distribution for $I$?

I'm examining a book. On pages 105 and 106 it is stated that:

For N-look intensity SAR images,  
$$I_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N I_1(i)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (x(i)^2+y(i)^2)$$  

Where $x(i)$ and $y(i)$ are the figures of the $i$th look (or sample). Since $x(i)$ and $y(i)$ are independently Gaussian distributed, it is well recognized that $NI_N$ possesses a Chi-square distribution with $2N$ degrees of freedom. Therefore, the PDF of the N-look intensity is illustrated by $$p_N(I)=\frac{N^N I^{N-1}}{(N-1)!\sigma^{2N}}\exp(-\frac{NI}{\sigma^2}),\quad I\ge 0$$  
The mean and the variance are $M_N(I)=\sigma^2$ and $\text{Var}_N(I)=\frac{\sigma^4}{N}$, respectively.

I don't have any trouble with $NI_N$ holding a chi-square distribution with $2N$ degrees of freedom but as we know the PDF for a chi-square distribution with $f$ degrees of freedom is:  
$$h(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2^{\frac{f}{2}}\Gamma(\frac{f}{2})}x^{\frac{(f-2)}{2}}e^{-\frac{x}{2}}\quad &, x\ge 0\\[2ex] 0\quad &, x\lt 0 \end{cases}$$  
so for the distribution of $NI$ we should have:  
$$p(NI)=\frac{1}{2^N\Gamma(N)}(NI)^{N-1}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})=\frac{N^{N-1}I^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})$$  
Then if we regard $Y=NI$ as a function of $I$, we have:  
$$p(Y)\,dY=p(I)\,dI\;,\;dY=N\,dI\\\frac{N^{N-1}I^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})NdI=p(I)dI\\p(I)=\frac{N^NI^{N-1}}{2^N(N-1)!}\exp(-\frac{NI}{2})$$  
Then where does that $\sigma^2$ derive from instead of $2$?  
As far as I understand degree of freedom ($f$) is the only parameter of chi-square distribution. and the mean and the variance of this distribution are $f$ and $2f$ respectively as wiki page explains.

I do not know the context, but I would speculate that gaussian distribution in the book are not scaled, so their variance is not equal to $1$. Therefore you have another parameter $\sigma^2$.  
So what you reveal is not exactly chi-squared distribution, but chi-squared scaled by a constant. Think of it as Gamma distribution with shape parameter $N$ and scale parameter $\sigma^2/N$.

A pyramid is a solid shape with  

• A polygon (a flat figure with straight edges) for a base  
• Slanting sides that are triangles that meet at the pinnacle (the top)  

Pyramids are one variety of polyhedron.  

The illustration shows a pentagonal pyramid, but you can use any polygon as the foundation of a pyramid. The most prevalent types of pyramids are triangular pyramids and square pyramids.  

### Description  

The purpose of this dictionary is to furnish definitions to common mathematical terms. Students acquire a new math skill every week at school, sometimes just prior to they start a new skill; if they wish to inspect what a specific term signifies, this is where this dictionary will become useful and a go-to reference for a student.  

### Audience  

Year 1 to Year 12 students  

### Learning Objectives  

Learn common math terms commencing with letter P

# Equality comparisons (C# Programming Manual)

It is sometimes essential to compare two values for congruence. In some situations, you are testing for value congruence, also known as equivalence, which signifies that the values that are held by the two variables are equal. In other instances, you have to ascertain whether two variables refer to the identical underlying object in memory. This type of equality is termed reference equality, or identity. This subject explains these two forms of equality and offers links to additional subjects for further information.

The second dual of a von Neumann algebra

Let $$A$$ be a von Neumann algebra and let $$A^{**}$$ be the second dual space of $$A$$.

Is this accurate that $$A^{**}=A$$ ?

No, it is in general not accurate. For instance, $$L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$$ is a von-Neumann algebra, but it is not a reflexive Banach space, that is, the second dual of $$L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$$ is not isomorphic to $$L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})$$.
It is likely accurate that being reflexive for von Neumann algebras implies being finite dimensional. Since every continuous linear map would be automatically weak-$$\ast$$ continuous, the weak-$$\ast$$ and norm topologies would have the same closed compact sets, but then the unit ball would be compact.

# Thabit numeral

In numeral theory, a Thabit numeral, Thâbit ibn Kurrah numeral, or 321 numeral is an integer of the form $3 \cdot 2^n - 1$ for a non-negative integer n.

The first few Thabit numerals are:

2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, 191, 383, 767, 1535, 3071, 6143, 12287, 24575, 49151, 98303, 196607, 393215, 786431, 1572863, ... (sequence A055010 in OEIS)

The 9th Century Iraqi Muslim mathematician, physician, astronomer and translator Thābit ibn Qurra is credited as the first to study these numerals and their relation to amicable numerals.

## Attributes

The binary representation of the Thabit numeral 3·2n−1 is n+2 digits long, consisting of "10" followed by n 1s.

The first few Thabit numerals that are prime (also known as 321 primes):

2, 5, 11, 23, 47, 191, 383, 6143, 786431, 51539607551, 824633720831, ... (sequence A007505 in OEIS)

As of April 2008, the known n values which give prime Thabit numerals are:

0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 11, 18, 34, 38, 43, 47, 55, 64, 76, 94, 103, 143, 206, 216, 306, 324, 391, 458, 470, 827, 1274, 3276, 4204, 5134, 7559, 12676, 14898, 18123, 18819, 25690, 26459, 41628, 51387, 71783, 80330, 85687, 88171, 97063, 123630, 155930, 164987, 234760, 414840, 584995, 702038, 727699, 992700, 1201046, 1232255, 2312734, 3136255 (sequence A002235 in OEIS)

The primes for n≥234760 were found by the distributed computing project 321 search. The largest of these, 3·24235414−1, has 1274988 digits and was found by Dylan Bennett in April 2008. The former record was 3·23136255−1 with 944108 digits, found by Paul Underwood in March 2007.

In 2008, Primegrid has taken over the search for Thabit primes. It is still searching and has already found Thabit primes for the following n:

4235414, 6090515

It is also searching for primes of the form 3·2n+1. Such primes occur for the following n:

2291610, 5082306, 7033641

## Connection with amicable numerals

When both n and n-1 yield prime Thabit numerals, and $9 \cdot 2^{2n - 1} - 1$ is also prime, a pair of amicable numerals can be calculated as follows:

$2^n(3 \cdot 2^{n - 1} - 1)(3 \cdot 2^n - 1)$ and $2^n(9 \cdot 2^{2n - 1} - 1).$

For example, n = 2 gives the Thabit numeral 11, and n = 1 gives the Thabit numeral 5, and our third term is 71. Then, 22=4, multiplied by 5 and 11 results in 220, whose divisors add up to 284, and 4 times 71 is 284, whose divisors add up to 220.

The only known n satisfying these conditions are 2, 4 and 7, corresponding to the Thabit numerals 11, 47 and 383.

3. ^ [2]
4. ^ [3]
5. ^ http://primes.utm.edu/bios/page.php?id=479
6. ^ http://primes.utm.edu/primes/lists/short.txt

Weight of Anhydrous Substance

1. Oct 5, 2009

### Predecessor

The dilemma statement, all factors and provided/recognized data
What is the weight of the anhydrous substance in $$Cu(NO_{3})_{2} * 2.5 H_{2}O$$
, in other words, the $$Cu(NO_{3})_{2}$$, if 4.875g of the hydrated substance is used?

The effort at a resolution
What I did was determine the formula weight of $$Cu(NO_{3})_{2}$$ which turned out to be 187.57g
Cu= 1 * 63.55 = 63.55
N= 2 * 14.01 = 28.02
O = 6 * 16.00 = 96.00

The formula weight of the water is 45.05g
H= 2.5(1.01 * 2) = 5.05g
O= 2.5(16.00 * 1) = 40g

From here I established a ratio:
4.875/232.62 = x/187.57
x = 3.931g of $$Cu(NO_{3})_{2}$$

Is this correct?

# XII Workshop on Particle Associations and Femtoscopy

Jun 12 – 16, 2017  
Other Institutions  
Europe/Zurich timezone  

## Resonance creation in small systems with ALICE  

Jun 15, 2017, 9:20 AM  
25m  
Other Institutions  

#### Other Institutions  

Nikhef Science Park 105 1098XG Amsterdam The Netherlands  

### Speaker  

Enrico Fragiacomo (Universita e INFN, Trieste (IT))  

### Description  

The creation of hadronic resonances such as K*(892)$^{0}$, $\phi$(1020), $\Sigma$(1385)$^{±}$, $\Lambda$(1520) and $\Xi(1530)^{0}$ has been evaluated as a function of multiplicity by the ALICE experiment in pp and p-Pb collisions at various energies at the LHC. These resonances vary by mass and strangeness content and thus can be utilized to provide insights on the mechanisms driving the recently observed multiplicity-dependent enhancement of strangeness creation in small systems. In this talk, we present new evaluations of resonance creation in pp collisions at $\sqrt{s}$ = 7 and 13 TeV as well as in p-Pb collisions at 5.02 TeV. Results include transverse momentum spectra, average $p_{\rm T}$, yield ratios to long-lasting hadrons in minimum bias collisions and as a function of multiplicity.  

List of tracks Resonance decays at low, intermediate and at RHIC and LHC  

### Primary author  

Enrico Fragiacomo (Universita e INFN, Trieste (IT))

Manipulating a set function [closed]  

I am experiencing difficulty utilizing Manipulate to create interactive plots.  

I handle equations that are relatively long. I would prefer to define them prior to employing them in Manipulate, and use their label in Manipulate instead of copying the whole equation for the function.  

For instance,  

I can effortlessly obtain the interactive plot for the subsequent function:  

Manipulate[Plot[Sin[a*x], {x, -5, 5}], {a, 0, 10}]  

However, if I attempt the equation below, I receive nothing. What am I executing incorrectly? I tried func1 := Sin[a*x];, but it doesn't alter anything.  

examplefunction = Sin[a*x];  
Manipulate[Plot[examplefunction, {x, -5, 5}], {a, 0, 10}]  

• You are nearly there. Define your function as: examplefunction[x_, a_] := Sin[a*x]; and then you can use Manipulate as follows: Manipulate[Plot[examplefunction[x, a], {x, -5, 5}], {a, 0, 10}]. Have fun! – Alexei Boulbitch Dec 3 '19 at 11:10  
• Thank you I got it functioning. I have a follow up question, if I =use instead of :=, it stills operates, why? – user68738 Dec 3 '19 at 11:21

This concern is elucidated in the Potential Issues section of documentation of Manipulate. 2. examplefunction[x_, a_] := and examplefunction[x_, a_] = are nearly equivalent in this scenario, for an advanced discussion check the following post: mathematica.stackexchange.com/q/181591/1871 – xzczd Dec 3 '19 at 11:40

# Steady Power and velocity of particle relation  

1. Mar 29, 2005  

### sAXIn  

Hello everyone  

I face a challenge resolving most straightforward issue pertaining to steady power and velocity of particle the issue is as follows:  

Express the velocity (V) of a car given a steady power P , the weight of the car is m, the car covers distance x and it at first was stationary.  

I presume initial velocity and dist. is zero, if P is steady I can express it as P=FV so  
V=P/F ; F=mA (where A is acceleration) here I sense there should be some integration but I don't know how to proceed ?  

Help will be valued!  

2. Mar 29, 2005  

### dextercioby  

Why do they provide you the distance "x"...? It necessitates a straightforward integration.  

$$P=m\frac{dv}{dt}v$$  

Do u see how to derive $v(t)$...?  

Daniel.  

3. Mar 29, 2005  

### sAXIn  

No I'm not so proficient with diff. equations.!  

4. Mar 29, 2005  

### dextercioby  

Separate elements and integrate with corresponding limits...  

$$v \ dv =\frac{P}{m} dt$$  

Daniel.  

5. Mar 29, 2005  

### sAXIn  

I think DX/DT is required ??/  

6. Mar 29, 2005  

### dextercioby  

It can't."x" provided in the issue is a numeral. I don't know why they provided it, though...  

Daniel.  

7. Mar 29, 2005  

### sAXIn  

I can post the response for you it turns out like : v=(3xp/m)^(1/3)!!!!  
The query is from Resnick Physics 1 4th edition chapter 7 problem 52 , I assume the response is accurate.  

8. Mar 29, 2005  

### dextercioby  

Okay the speed is  

$$v=\sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}} \sqrt{t}$$ (1)  

Integrate wrt time & utilize the initial condition (t=0,x=0) to determine  

$$x=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2P}{m}} \ t^{\frac{3}{2}}$$ (2)
